blocks.text: Learn every noun with its article and plural: der Tisch - die Tische.
The rule

German nouns begin with a capital letter. Each noun has a grammatical gender: masculine, feminine or neuter. The definite article means “the”; the indefinite article usually means “a/an”. The forms below are nominative.
Common plural patterns
Examples

blocks.de: Das ist ein Buch. Das Buch ist neu.
blocks.en: This is a book. The book is new.
I am buying books.

blocks.text: Watch out
There is no single plural rule for every noun. Grammatical gender is not the same as natural gender: das Mädchen means “the girl”.
Use pronouns to identify who is speaking or acting. Learn sein (to be) and haben (to have) early.
The rule
The verb changes to match the subject. Use du for one person addressed informally, ihr for more than one, and Sie for formal address. Formal Sie can be singular or plural and is always capitalised.
Examples

blocks.en: I am a university student.
We have time today.
Do you have a question? (formal)

blocks.de: Das Buch ist neu. Es ist interessant.
blocks.en: The book is new. It is interesting.

blocks.text: Watch out
Use sein for age: Ich bin 25 Jahre alt. German says Ich habe Hunger for “I am hungry”. An unmodified profession after sein often has no article: Er ist Arzt.
Use the present tense for current actions, habits and facts. It can also describe future plans when the time is clear.
The rule
For many verbs, remove -en from the infinitive and add a personal ending: lernen → lern-.
Patterns to remember
Many stems ending in -t or -d add -e- before -st or -t: du arbeitest. With verbs such as heißen, say du heißt, not “heißst”.
Some verbs change their vowel in du and er/sie/es: fahren → fährst/fährt, lesen → liest/liest, essen → isst/isst. Learn these with the verb.
Examples

blocks.en: I study German every day.
She is reading a message right now.
I am going to Berlin tomorrow.

blocks.text: Watch out
German has no separate everyday present-progressive form. Ich lerne can mean “I study” or “I am studying”, depending on context.
Recognise where the finite verb goes. “Finite” means the verb form that agrees with the subject.
The rule

In an ordinary statement, the finite verb is the second sentence element. The first element can contain several words. If another element comes first, the subject normally follows the verb in simple A1 sentences.
Question patterns
wer = who; was = what; wo = where; woher = where from; wohin = where to; wann = when; wie = how; warum = why.
Examples

blocks.en: Today I am studying German.
Do you have time?
Where are you from?

blocks.text: Watch out
German does not add “do/does” to form these questions. Say Arbeitest du heute? Second position does not mean second word: Am Montag is one element.
Use the nominative for the subject. Many common verbs take an accusative object: haben, kaufen, brauchen, sehen.
The rule
With these articles, only the masculine form changes between nominative and accusative. Ask wer? to identify the subject and wen oder was? to identify an accusative object.
Examples

blocks.en: The man buys a coffee.
I need a bag.
There is a supermarket here.

blocks.text: Useful pattern: es gibt + accusative
Es gibt means “there is / there are”. The noun phrase that follows is accusative: Es gibt einen Park. / Es gibt zwei Parks.
Watch out
Sein does not take an accusative object. Say Er ist ein Lehrer when using an article, not “einen Lehrer”. Cases belong to phrases, not fixed positions: the first noun is not always the subject.
Use possessive articles before a noun to say who something belongs to: my, your, his, her, our and their.
The rule
The owner determines the stem. The noun that follows determines the ending through gender, number and case. Possessives follow the pattern of ein, with an additional plural form.
Examples

blocks.en: I am visiting my brother.
Is that your bag? (informal plural)

blocks.text: Watch out
Euer normally loses its second e when an ending is added: eure, euren, eurem. Formal Ihr is capitalised. Dative forms include meinem, meiner, meinem, meinen.
Choose the negative form according to what you are negating.
The rule
Use kein to negate a noun that would have ein/eine or no article. Use nicht to negate an adjective, a particular phrase or an action/statement.
The forms of kein
Kein follows the endings of ein and also has plural forms: kein Mann, keine Frau, kein Kind, keine Bücher. Accusative masculine: keinen Mann.
Where does nicht go?
Put it directly before a specific adjective or phrase you want to negate. When negating the whole action, it often comes later, but before a final infinitive or separable prefix.

blocks.de: Ich fahre nicht nach Berlin, sondern nach Bonn.
blocks.en: I am not going to Berlin, but to Bonn.
I cannot come today.
I am not calling today.
I do not have time.

blocks.text: Watch out
Do not learn “nicht always goes at the end”. Its position depends on scope and sentence structure. Compare nicht teuer (not expensive) and keinen Kaffee (no coffee).
Express ability, permission, obligation and intention. Use möchte for a polite wish.
The rule
The modal verb is finite and takes second position in a statement. The main verb stays in the infinitive at the end, without zu.

blocks.en: I can swim well.
We have to work today.
I would like to drink a tea.

blocks.text: Two more useful verbs

sollen = be supposed to / should: ich soll, du sollst, er soll, wir sollen, ihr sollt, sie sollen.
mögen = like: ich mag, du magst, er mag, wir mögen, ihr mögt, sie mögen. Ich mag Tee. = I like tea.
Watch out

Du musst nicht kommen. = You do not have to come.
Du darfst nicht kommen. = You must not come.
Möchte is a polite-wish form of mögen; learn it as a useful A1 pattern.
Some verbs have a prefix that separates in a simple main clause: anrufen, aufstehen, einkaufen, mitkommen.
The rule
Conjugate the verb and put it in the normal finite-verb position. Move the separable prefix to the end of the clause.
With a modal verb
Keep the infinitive together at the end. Only the modal verb is conjugated.

blocks.en: I have to get up early.
Can you call me tomorrow?

blocks.text: The sentence frame

blocks.en: I am calling my sister this evening.

blocks.text: The two verb parts form a frame around the other information. A similar frame appears with the perfect tense.
Watch out
Not every prefix separates. Common inseparable prefixes include be-, ver-, er-, ent-, emp-, ge-, miss-, zer-: Ich besuche meine Eltern. Learn whether a new verb is separable.
Use the imperative for instructions, invitations and requests. Add bitte for politeness.
The rule
For du, many verbs allow a final -e: Komm! or Komme! Some need it, such as Arbeite! Irregular verbs need special attention.
Examples

blocks.en: Please open the window. (formal)
Please call me! (informal singular)
Please be on time! (informal plural)

blocks.text: A softer request

blocks.en: Can you speak more slowly, please?

blocks.text: Watch out
Omit du and ihr in the normal imperative pattern; keep Sie in the formal form. Special forms of sein: sei / seid / seien Sie.
Recognise the dative after common verbs and prepositions. With “give”, it often identifies the recipient.
The rule
Learn the case with the verb or preposition. Common dative verbs include helfen (help), danken (thank) and gefallen (appeal to / be liked by).
Examples

blocks.en: I help the child.
I like the book. Literally: the book appeals to me.
I give the woman a pen.

blocks.text: In the last example, der Frau is the dative recipient and einen Stift is the accusative thing given.
Common dative prepositions
mit (with), bei (at/with), von (from/of), zu (to), aus (from/out of), nach (to/after), seit (since/for).

blocks.en: I travel by bus.

blocks.text: Watch out
Dative plural nouns usually add -n: die Kinder → mit den Kindern. Do not add another -n if the plural already ends in -n, or if it ends in -s: mit den Frauen / mit den Autos.
Replace a known person or thing with a pronoun. Its form depends on the case required by the sentence.
The rule
Use an accusative pronoun with an accusative verb or preposition, and a dative pronoun with a dative verb or preposition. A thing can be replaced by a pronoun matching its grammatical gender.
Examples

blocks.en: I see Anna. I see her.
I help Anna. I help her.

blocks.de: Der Kaffee ist gut. Ich trinke ihn.
blocks.en: The coffee is good. I drink it.

blocks.de: Das ist für dich. Ich komme mit dir.
blocks.en: This is for you. I am coming with you.

blocks.text: Watch out
Für takes accusative; mit takes dative. Both mich and mir can translate as “me”. Formal Sie and Ihnen stay capitalised.
Distinguish where something is (wo?) from its destination (wohin?). Learn common travel phrases as units.
Two-way prepositions: the basic contrast

in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen can take dative or accusative. For the basic spatial pattern: use dative for location, and accusative for a destination or change of spatial relation.

blocks.en: I am in the park. (location; in dem)
I am going into/to the park. (destination)
I am running in the park. (within a location)

blocks.text: Common contractions
im = in dem; ins = in das; am = an dem; ans = an das; zum = zu dem; zur = zu der; beim = bei dem; vom = von dem.
Watch out
Movement alone does not mean accusative. Zu always takes dative: zum Bahnhof. Countries with articles use other patterns: in die Türkei (to), in der Türkei (in).
Use a time phrase to say when, how often or for how long something happens.

rows: von neun bis zwölf / nine to twelve
nach dem Kurs / after the course
seit einem Jahr / for a year
vor einem Jahr / a year ago

blocks.text: The rule
Use the present tense with seit when a situation started in the past and still continues. English often uses “have been” or “have lived” in the same situation.
Examples

blocks.de: Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in Trier.
blocks.en: I have lived in Trier for a year.
The course starts at nine o’clock.

blocks.de: Ich lerne jeden Tag. Ich bleibe zwei Tage.
blocks.en: I study every day. I am staying for two days.

blocks.text: Frequency
immer = always; oft = often; manchmal = sometimes; selten = rarely; nie = never. Ich koche oft. = I often cook.
Watch out
No preposition is needed with heute, morgen, gestern or jeden Tag. Compare am Montag (on Monday) and montags (on Mondays).
Describe people and things, and say what you like doing. Start with adjectives after sein and common everyday comparisons.
The rule
An adjective after sein does not take a gender or plural ending. An adjective describing how an action is performed also stays unchanged in these basic patterns.

blocks.de: Der Kaffee ist heiß. Die Suppe ist heiß.
blocks.en: The coffee is hot. The soup is hot.
The books are interesting.
She speaks slowly.

blocks.text: Liking things and activities
Useful forms to recognise

gut - besser - am besten = good/well - better - best.
viel - mehr - am meisten = much/a lot - more - most.
gern - lieber - am liebsten = like doing - prefer - like best.

blocks.de: Dieses Zimmer ist größer als mein Zimmer.
blocks.en: This room is bigger than my room.

blocks.text: Watch out
Adjectives before a noun need endings: ein kleiner Tisch, eine kleine Tasche. Recognise common phrases at this stage; full adjective declension and comparison are later topics.
Connect short statements without losing the main-clause word order.

rows: Ich lerne, aber ich bin müde.
Kommst du oder bleibst du hier?
Ich bleibe hier, denn ich bin müde.
Das ist kein Tee, sondern Kaffee.

blocks.text: The rule

These coordinating conjunctions do not occupy the first position of the following clause. The finite verb keeps its normal main-clause position. Use a comma before aber, denn and sondern. Use sondern to replace something just negated.
Examples

blocks.de: Ich trinke Tee, aber meine Schwester trinkt Kaffee.
blocks.en: I drink tea, but my sister drinks coffee.

blocks.de: Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich bin müde.
blocks.en: I am going home because I am tired.
I am buying bread and milk.

blocks.text: Then: dann
Dann is an adverb. When it starts a statement, it takes first position and the finite verb follows.

blocks.de: Ich frühstücke. Dann gehe ich zur Arbeit.
blocks.en: I have breakfast. Then I go to work.

blocks.text: Watch out
Do not transfer this pattern to weil. Unlike denn, weil introduces a subordinate clause with a verb-final pattern. That is a separate later topic in this review sequence.
Use the perfect tense (Perfekt) to talk about completed past events in everyday conversation.
The rule
Use a present-tense form of haben or sein plus a past participle (Partizip II). In a statement, the auxiliary is in second position and the participle is at the end.

blocks.en: I studied German yesterday.

blocks.text: Examples

blocks.en: We went shopping yesterday.
She studied at university in Bonn.
Did you work today?

blocks.text: The auxiliary changes; the participle does not
ich habe gelernt, du hast gelernt, wir haben gelernt. The auxiliary agrees with the subject; the participle stays the same.
Watch out
The pattern ge-...-t is not universal. Strong and mixed verbs have forms such as gesehen and gebracht. Learn the participle and auxiliary with each verb.

title: The perfect tense: haben or sein?

blocks.text: Learn common past forms as a pair: hat gemacht, ist gegangen. This is more reliable than guessing.
The rule
Most verbs use haben. Many intransitive verbs of travel or change of state use sein. Sein and bleiben also use sein. Not every movement verb takes sein.
Examples

blocks.en: We went to Cologne.
I drank a coffee.

blocks.text: Watch out
Choose the auxiliary for the meaning and construction. Ich bin nach Bonn gefahren describes travel; Ich habe das Auto gefahren has a direct object and uses haben.

title: Talking about the past: war & hatte

blocks.text: In everyday German, the simple past of sein and haben is very common, even when other verbs use the perfect tense.
The rule
These are finite past-tense verbs. Do not add a second auxiliary. Use them for past states, locations and possession.
Examples

blocks.en: Yesterday I was tired.
We were in Berlin at the weekend.
I did not have time yesterday.
Were you at home?

blocks.text: Present and past
Watch out
Use ich hatte, not “ich habe hatte”. Perfect forms such as ich bin gewesen are also grammatical, but war and hatte are especially useful for simple everyday accounts.
Use numbers for quantities, prices and time. Use ordinal numbers for dates.
Building numbers
From 21 to 99, say the unit before the ten: einundzwanzig (21), vierunddreißig (34). Notice sechzehn (16), siebzehn (17), dreißig (30), sechzig (60), siebzig (70).
Dates
Many ordinals from 1 to 19 end in -te; from 20 onward use -ste. Key irregular forms: erste, dritte, siebte, achte. After am, use a dative ending.

blocks.en: Today is the third of May.
The appointment is on the third of May.

blocks.text: Useful fixed patterns

blocks.de: Wie viel kostet das? / Wie viele Bücher hast du?
blocks.en: How much does that cost? / How many books do you have?
It is cold. / It is raining.

blocks.text: Watch out
Halb neun means 8:30, not 9:30. Use wie viele with countable plural nouns. In weather expressions, keep the subject es.
